deep.reconstruction:
This page has no derivation and no handwriting by Gauss. It is printed text, p. v of the preface (Vorrede) of an arithmetic/algebra textbook, almost certainly Christian Leiste's 'Die Arithmetik und Algebra' (Wolfenbüttel, 1790), from Gauss's library (bundle 'HB.Leiste'). It continues the author's short history of the subject for his pupils. Its claims:
(1) Ordinary people solve small 'algebraic' problems in their heads without instruction, so arithmetic and algebra predate any named inventor. Astronomers and reckoners existed before history names one.
(2) The Bible already contains computations with whole numbers and fractions.
(3) Peoples with an alphabetic script wrote numbers with letters 'according to the decadic law' (§4 of the book: base-10 place value / decimal grouping). Peoples with pictographic script used pictures. 'Our common digits' are such pictographs, received from the Arabs in the 10th century AD. The Arabs had them from the Indians, as Johannes de Sacrobosco and others testify.
(4) Multiplication and division of large numbers are therefore old. The author doubts that Pythagoras of Samos invented the multiplication table (Einmaleins, §11) c. 550 BC. He thinks it likely that Pythagoras introduced the polygonal numbers. He says Pythagoras, like all later mathematicians, worked much with irrational numbers (§45), especially square and cube roots.
The sentence ends on the next page: such roots can only be approximated arithmetically, which motivated geometric constructions.

The only implicit mathematics is the notion of polygonal numbers. In modern form, the n-th k-gonal number is P(k,n) = ((k-2)n^2 - (k-4)n)/2. This formula is my gloss; it is not on the page.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there are no derivations.

Historical judgments are of 18th-century standard. Attributing work on irrationals and cube roots to Pythagoras himself, rather than to later Pythagoreans (e.g. Hippasus, Theodorus), is not supported by modern scholarship.
The 'Pythagorean table' (mensa Pythagorica) attribution of the multiplication table is legendary, transmitted via Boethius-era tradition. The author is right to doubt it.
'Received from the Arabs in the 10th century' reflects the Gerbert tradition (c. 980). Wide adoption came much later, via Fibonacci (1202) and the algorism literature including Sacrobosco (c. 1230).

results.what: Historical remark: Hindu-Arabic numerals came to Europe from the Arabs, who had them from India (citing Sacrobosco)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard historiography (Sacrobosco's Algorismus, c. 1230; Gerbert of Aurillac, 10th c.)

results.what: Attribution of polygonal numbers to Pythagoras
Doubt about Pythagoras inventing the multiplication table

deep.surprise_reason: This is a printed page of Leiste's textbook preface containing only conventional historical narrative. There are no annotations or mathematics by Gauss.

checkable.asserts: The polygonal-number formula with k=3 gives the triangular numbers n(n+1)/2 (difference simplifies to 0); my gloss on the 'Polygonal-Zahlen' mentioned.
The polygonal-number formula with k=4 gives the squares n^2.

transcription_corrections: The page number is a lowercase roman 'v' at top right.
Signature mark at bottom reads '*3' and the catchword is 'Weil'.

'Ein mal eins', 'Pythagoras', 'Polygonal=Zahlen', 'Irrational=Zahlen', 'decadischen Gesetze', 'Bilderschrift', 'Ziffern' and 'Johann de Sacro Bosco' are set in a heavier/emphasis typeface (Schwabacher or bold), not captured in the transcription.
